what_its_for: Olanzapine is used to treat certain mental health conditions including schizophrenia (a condition that affects how you think, feel, and behave) and bipolar disorder (also called manic-depressive illness, which causes extreme mood swings). It may also be used with other medicines to treat depression. It works by helping to balance certain natural chemicals in your brain.
how_to_take: Take olanzapine exactly as your doctor prescribes. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the regular tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you have the orally disintegrating tablet (Zyprexa Zydis), open the blister pack with dry hands, place the tablet on your tongue, and let it dissolve — do not chew or crush it. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better, as stopping too quickly can cause your symptoms to return.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how well it works for you and how you feel. Typical starting doses are 5 to 10 mg once daily. Most people take it once a day, usually at bedtime, since it can make you sleepy. Never take more than your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose without asking your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store olanzapine tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture — do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the orally disintegrating tablets in their sealed blister packs until you are ready to use them. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine that is expired — check the expiration date on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking olanzapine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and may cause dangerous side effects. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires full alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting overheated or dehydrated — drink plenty of water, especially in hot weather or during exercise, as olanzapine can make it harder for your body to cool down. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this can cause dizziness or fainting. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, as olanzapine can interact with many other drugs.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: high fever, stiff muscles, confusion, or sweating (these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); uncontrollable movements of your face, tongue, or body (called tardive dyskinesia); thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; severe dizziness or fainting; difficulty swallowing; signs of infection such as fever or sore throat; or yellowing of your skin or eyes. Also contact your doctor if you notice significant weight gain, feel extremely restless or unable to sit still, or if your symptoms get worse.
when_it_works: Olanzapine does not work immediately. You may start to notice some improvement in sleep or agitation within the first few days. However, it may take 2 to 4 weeks or longer to feel the full benefits of the medicine. It is very important to keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you do not notice changes right away. Do not give up too soon — be patient and keep your follow-up appointments so your doctor can check your progress.
special_populations: Older adults: Older people, especially those with dementia, have a higher risk of serious side effects including stroke and death. Talk to your doctor about the risks. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Taking olanzapine during the last trimester of pregnancy may cause withdrawal symptoms or breathing problems in newborns. Breastfeeding: Olanzapine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children and teenagers: This medicine may be prescribed to children aged 13 and older for certain conditions, but children may be more sensitive to side effects like weight gain. Regular monitoring by a doctor is very important. Diabetes: Olanzapine can raise blood sugar levels. If you have diabetes or are at risk for it, your doctor will monitor your blood sugar closely.
